facts.fact_text: The first applicant (Mr Aristov) and the second applicant (Mr Gromov) took part in the demonstration on 6 May 2012 at Bolotnaya Square.
The first applicant (Mr Aristov) and the second applicant (Mr Gromov) were arrested at the venue of the demonstration on 6 May 2012.
According to the second applicant (Mr Gromov), on 6 May 2012 at 4 p.m. he came to Bolotnaya Square to participate in the authorised demonstration.

According to the second applicant (Mr Gromov), at that moment a few police officers ran out of the cordon and arrested State Duma Deputy Ponomarev and everyone around him, including the second applicant (Mr Gromov).
The first applicant (Mr Aristov) and the second applicant (Mr Gromov) were arrested at the venue of the demonstration on 6 May 2012.
After their arrest, the first applicant (Mr Aristov) and the second applicant (Mr Gromov) were brought to police stations where they were charged with administrative offences.
After an overnight detention, the first applicant (Mr Aristov) and the second applicant (Mr Gromov) were brought before the justices of the peace and convicted as charged.
At 9.20 p.m. on 6 May 2012 the second applicant (Mr Gromov) was administratively arrested at Veshnyaki district police station.
On 7 May 2012 the second applicant (Mr Gromov) was brought before the Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow.
The first applicant (Mr Aristov) was accused of having disobeyed a lawful order of the police, an offence under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The second applicant (Mr Gromov) was accused of having disobeyed a lawful order of the police, an offence under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
According to the Government, the first applicant (Mr Aristov) was arrested because he had disregarded police orders to cease his actions at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012.
According to the Government, the second applicant (Mr Gromov) was arrested because he had disregarded the police order to cease breaking the police cordon and to disperse.
When the marchers arrived at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012, it became apparent that barriers installed by the police had narrowed the entrance to the meeting venue.
The barriers installed by the police at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012 allegedly restricted the space allocated for the meeting.
To control the crowd at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012, a police cordon forced the protestors to remain within the barriers.
There were numerous clashes between the police and protesters at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012.
At 5.30 p.m. on 6 May 2012 the police ordered that the meeting at Bolotnaya Square finish early.
At 5.30 p.m. on 6 May 2012 the police began to disperse the participants of the demonstration at Bolotnaya Square.
According to the first applicant (Mr Aristov), he did not cause any disorder at the time of his apprehension on 6 May 2012.
According to the first applicant (Mr Aristov), he did not resist the police officers who arrested him on 6 May 2012.
According to the first applicant (Mr Aristov), the police officers who arrested him on 6 May 2012 gave no orders during his arrest.

Before the Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow, the first applicant (Mr Aristov) insisted that he had not broken the police cordon and had been arrested by the police with no warnings or orders.

The first applicant (Mr Aristov) applied to have the two police officers who had arrested him examined as witnesses before the Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow.

The Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow rejected the first applicant's (Mr Aristov's) application to have the two arresting police officers examined as witnesses, in order to expedite the proceedings.

The Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow dismissed as unreliable the testimony of defence witnesses, who stated that the first applicant (Mr Aristov) had not chanted any slogans in their presence and had not participated in breaking the cordon.

The Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow dismissed the video recording submitted by the first applicant (Mr Aristov) on the grounds that it showed the background of the events in question rather than the applicant's arrest.

The Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka District of Moscow dismissed the video recording submitted by the first applicant (Mr Aristov) on the additional grounds that it did not contain any sound and could not therefore prove whether the applicant had chanted any slogans or not.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow rejected the first applicant's (Mr Aristov's) application to summon and question the two arresting police officers owing to the applicant's failure to name those officers.
The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow questioned two defence witnesses who confirmed the first applicant's (Mr Aristov's) account of events but stated that they had not observed his arrest.
The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow dismissed the testimony of the two defence witnesses as unreliable because both witnesses were the first applicant's (Mr Aristov's) friends.

The second applicant's (Mr Gromov's) sister confirmed his account of events — that he had come closer to listen to State Duma Deputy Ponomarev and was arrested along with those around the deputy — but the Justice of the Peace of Court Circuit no. 114 of the Luberetskiy Court District of Moscow Region dismissed her statements as unreliable evidence.
The second applicant (Mr Gromov) appealed against the judgment of 14 August 2012, pointing out that he had been arrested by riot squad officers rather than by Officers D. and S.
On 24 September 2012 the Lyuberetskiy Town Court of the Moscow Region examined the second applicant's (Mr Gromov's) appeal against the judgment of 14 August 2012.
The Lyuberetskiy Town Court of the Moscow Region dismissed the second applicant's (Mr Gromov's) allegations that he had been arrested by riot squad officers rather than by Officers D. and S.

The Lyuberetskiy Town Court of the Moscow Region considered that the statements of Officers D. and S. about the second applicant's (Mr Gromov's) failure to obey their lawful demands to stop marching after the end of the event had been trustworthy.
